extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific inquiry; philosophers of science; readers studying logic and induction
extracted.subtask_description: Identify common à priori fallacies and natural prejudices that mislead investigation of the laws of nature, with guidance and historical examples showing how to avoid them and rely on experience instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for the most familiar/simple hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that the most familiar explanation or hypothesis must be the truest; favouring simple or familiar suppositions (e.g., circular motion or revolving spheres for heavenly bodies) because they seem simplest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept a hypothesis merely because it is familiar or simple; beware of adding ad hoc complications ("sphere to sphere and circle to circle") to force a familiar theory to fit contradicting facts. Let empirical contradictions guide revision rather than preserving apparent simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reification of abstractions / personification of general terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating names of qualities or general terms as if they denote separate entities (e.g., treating 'whiteness' or 'man in general' as distinct objective substances or Universal Substances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that names of qualities and names of substances may refer to the same sets of facts under different relations; avoid assuming that every linguistic generality corresponds to a distinct external entity. Avoid mysticism that ascribes objective existence to subjective ideas or abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whatever can be thought of apart exists apart
rubrics_metrics.description: The a priori prejudice that whatever can be conceived separately must exist separately in the world—leading to personification and ontological inflation of abstractions (Fate, Chance, Nature, Time, Space as beings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't infer independent external existence from conceptual separability or linguistic convenience. Treat generalizations as descriptions, not as evidence of distinct metaphysical substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of the Sufficient Reason used à priori
rubrics_metrics.description: Asserting a phenomenon must follow a particular law because we see no reason it should deviate (e.g., arguing a body at rest cannot begin to move because there's 'no reason' for one direction rather than another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is fallacious when used without empirical support. Refrain from deducing laws from the mere absence of imagined alternatives; rely on experience to determine whether any such reason exists. The real proof of laws of motion or other laws is empirical consistency with facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming one single cause (neglecting plurality of causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tacit assumption (e.g., in Bacon’s methodology) that a phenomenon has a single, invariable 'forma' or cause present in all instances of that phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume unity of cause for phenomena—especially sensible qualities—which often depend on an unassignable variety of distinct causes. Consider plurality of causes and investigate effects of given causes experimentally rather than seeking a single cause of an effect by elimination alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferring nature from our mental distinctions / linguistic categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Believing that differences in nature must correspond to received distinctions in language or common phraseology; treating linguistic classes as natural classes (e.g., relying on popular phrases to form scientific classes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting accidental features of a language determine scientific classification. Distinguish between the convenience of common speech and the actual relations among natural phenomena; base classifications on observed facts, not on ordinary language distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of contrarieties (deriving natural oppositions from language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming that oppositions apparent in words or abstract conception (limited/unlimited, odd/even, rest/motion, etc.) correspond to fundamental antitheses in nature and can be used to deduce natural laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not elevate linguistic or abstract oppositions into proofs of natural principles. Use observation and experiment to test whether such oppositions reflect real natural contrasts rather than assuming them a priori.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deriving physical laws by pure geometry or à priori reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to prove general physical facts solely by logical or geometrical reasoning without appeal to experiment (e.g., attempts by Archimedes or some geometers to deduce statics entirely à priori).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer empirical evidence where available. If a conclusion about physical reality can be safely appealed to experience, do not substitute purely à priori proofs for experimental confirmation—especially when such proofs tacitly rely on unproven premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaking order of inquiry: seeking causes of effects vs. effects of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking the primary scientific problem to be 'what is the cause of a given effect' rather than 'what are the effects of a given cause', which limits the productive use of experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus experimental inquiry on discovering the effects of specified causes (which can be more directly and reliably probed), since producing an effect artificially gives evidence about causes. Avoid overemphasis on devising crucial instances to isolate a single cause of a complex effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming resemblance between causes and effects (like-produces-like fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deep prejudice that the conditions of a phenomenon must resemble the phenomenon itself; that causes must necessarily resemble their effects (e.g., Doctrine of Signatures, belief that elements' properties resemble properties of their compounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not select hypotheses or interventions based solely on superficial resemblance to the desired effect. Historical examples (charms, Doctrine of Signatures, attempts to infer elements' properties from compounds) show this leads to error. Base causal inferences on observation and experiment rather than analogical appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflating phenomena with their conditions or causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Using language that identifies a phenomenon with the conditions that produce it (e.g., saying 'heat is a kind of motion' without distinguishing the sensation from its physical conditions), leading to confusion between effect and cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain conceptual clarity: distinguish the observed phenomenon from the physical conditions or processes that produce it. Avoid defining the phenomenon as identical with its supposed cause; test causal hypotheses empirically and keep descriptive and explanatory language distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assuming perception must resemble external objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The expectation that mental impressions or ideas must closely resemble external objects (e.g., Epicurean species sensibiles or doctrines that ideas are animal motions of organs), leading to mistaken theories of perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that sensations or mental representations need not be copies of their causes. Avoid building explanatory systems that presuppose pictorial resemblance between cause and effect in perception; instead, argue and test whether perceptual processes require resemblance.
